item.text: {"chapter_id":"3B","answers":[{"question_id":"3B.1","answer":"Protection from state abuse was materially inadequate but mixed. The government had formal protections: a victim-reparation law provided legal assistance, witness protection, health care, compensation, and guarantees of non-repetition, while 2023 legislation and justice-capacity measures supported human-rights and penitentiary protections, magistrate recruitment, mobile courts, and selected convictions (BATCH-0029-E001; BATCH-0029-E002; BATCH-0009-E004). The government also reported prosecutions of security personnel after the Goma killings and released Franck Diongo without charge, but those actions do not establish lawful initial detention, discipline, or nationwide remedy (BATCH-0011-E021; BATCH-0003-E007). Contrary evidence included 2023 reports of arbitrary killings, enforced disappearance, torture, harsh prisons, arbitrary detention, political detainees, and continuing impunity, with UN access denied to some military and intelligence detention facilities (BATCH-0011-E008; BATCH-0011-E014). In Goma, security forces killed dozens, arrested civilians, and military authorities conducted incomplete investigations and flawed prosecutions; four security personnel were convicted, but victim identification, forensic work, witness participation, appeals, and reparations remained incomplete or uncertain (BATCH-0011-E018; BATCH-0011-E020; BATCH-0011-E021). A separate Kisangani victims’ protest was allegedly met with police beatings, humiliation, theft, and abduction while compensation remained unresolved (BATCH-0022-E009). Some severe violence was committed by armed groups, so it cannot be attributed personally to Tshisekedi absent command or notice evidence. The target-period record therefore shows recurring state-attributed abuse with partial formal protection and limited accountability, not effective protection or verified remedy.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0029-E001","BATCH-0029-E002","BATCH-0009-E004","BATCH-0011-E018","BATCH-0011-E020","BATCH-0011-E021","BATCH-0022-E009"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0003-E007","BATCH-0011-E014","BATCH-0011-E008","BATCH-0026-E008"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Personal presidential ordering is not established for each detention, killing, or police incident.","Formal laws, prosecutions, and convictions do not demonstrate consistent national enforcement or completed reparations.","The evidence does not provide a complete national series for disappearances, torture, detention conditions, or abuse prevalence.","Armed-group violence and conflict conditions are important external causes.","Some casualty, investigation, and judicial findings remained disputed or incomplete."]},{"question_id":"3B.2","answer":"Tshisekedi possessed formal authority over coercive institutions and issued preventive directives, including messages to frontline troops, instructions that the FARDC defend the population, and appointments of defense, interior, and security officials; the government also reported commander commitments, military ethics training, judicial-police training, and police-investigation reforms (BATCH-0006-E001; BATCH-0019-E010; BATCH-0009-E003; BATCH-0011-E004; BATCH-0009-E005). These records establish appointments, stated intent, or institutional activity, but not adequate resourcing, implementation, discipline, or nationwide results. Contrary evidence shows FARDC soldiers arrested and beat journalists without a documented final disciplinary outcome, security forces killed civilians, and surrendered Mobondo fighters were transferred into military training without vetting for prior abuses (BATCH-0026-E007; BATCH-0010-E015). Human Rights Watch also reported that the administration supported Wazalendo and FDLR forces, contracted private military personnel, and used armed groups alongside government troops, creating risks of impunity and further abuse (BATCH-0028-E016; BATCH-0011-E019). The Goma operation involved planned military orders, lethal force, mass arrests, and incomplete command accountability; some officers were convicted, but the evidence does not establish that Tshisekedi personally ordered or approved the operation (BATCH-0011-E018; BATCH-0011-E022). Attribution is strongest for national appointments, security strategy, and administration-level support for aligned actors; it is weaker for individual provincial, unit, or battlefield conduct. Overall, formal control and some corrective activity coexisted with recurring failures to prevent, vet, investigate, or discipline coercive abuse.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0006-E001","BATCH-0019-E010","BATCH-0009-E003","BATCH-0011-E004","BATCH-0009-E005","BATCH-0026-E007","BATCH-0010-E015","BATCH-0028-E016"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0011-E018","BATCH-0011-E021","BATCH-0011-E022","BATCH-0011-E003"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The evidence does not establish operational control over every unit or aligned group.","Official training, codes, and claimed reductions in abuse are not independently quantified here.","The effectiveness of appointments and police or military reforms is not demonstrated.","Provincial command responsibility must be distinguished from personal presidential responsibility.","The Goma findings are investigative and advocacy conclusions, not final findings against Tshisekedi."]},{"question_id":"3B.3","answer":"The evidence is mixed and does not establish direct presidential incitement of domestic protected groups. Tshisekedi publicly endorsed love, unity, equality, and opposition to divisiveness, and described legal prohibitions on ethnic, racial, tribal, and xenophobic hate speech (BATCH-0020-E015; BATCH-0016-E003). Conversely, he said he would target without hesitation or regret people he regarded as threats to national security, warned against alleged foreign influence in the election, and used hostile rhetoric toward Rwanda and M23; the latter concerned an external armed conflict and is not by itself domestic incitement (BATCH-0003-E010; BATCH-0018-E007; BATCH-0007-E013). During the campaign, a UDPS governor made a statement that CSAC deemed ethnic-regional incitement, while UDPS supporters were implicated in attacks on opposition supporters, journalists, and political actors; Kasumbalesa violence included reported injuries and sexual assaults, with no known investigation at the time (BATCH-0002-E017; BATCH-0010-E021; BATCH-0002-E014). The 2023 human-rights assessment also described hate speech and ethnic violence in the national environment, but does not prove presidential authorship or endorsement (BATCH-0011-E008). Tshisekedi’s responsibility for aligned officials’ or supporters’ conduct is therefore limited by uncertain command, notice, and remedy evidence. The record supports concern about hostile security rhetoric and an insufficiently controlled party environment, but not a proven personal causal chain from presidential speech to domestic physical harm.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0020-E015","BATCH-0016-E003","BATCH-0003-E010","BATCH-0002-E017","BATCH-0002-E014","BATCH-0010-E021"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0018-E007","BATCH-0007-E013","BATCH-0011-E008","BATCH-0010-E021"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The evidence does not show whether Tshisekedi disciplined the governor or party supporters after notice.","Presidential endorsement of the reported attacks is not established.","The causal effect of the rhetoric on subsequent violence is unknown.","External-conflict rhetoric should not be converted into domestic incitement without a physical-safety nexus.","The evidence is concentrated in the 2023 campaign period."]},{"question_id":"3B.4","answer":"The government created and operated formal accountability mechanisms, but independence and effective remedy were limited. Positive evidence includes a victim-reparation commission and fund, magistrate recruitment and training, mobile courts, a National Commission on Human Rights that visited detention centers and followed complaints, police-investigation capacity building, and an ICC cooperation agreement (BATCH-0029-E001; BATCH-0009-E004; BATCH-0011-E014; BATCH-0009-E005; BATCH-0019-E001). The government also prosecuted some security personnel, including convictions related to Goma, and supported an inquiry into alleged FARDC violence (BATCH-0011-E003; BATCH-0011-E021). These are institutional outputs or formal commitments, not proof of independent operation or completed remedy. Contrary evidence includes judicial and military interference, corruption, resource shortages, denial of UN access to some detention sites, weak provincial coverage of oversight bodies, and allegations that authorities failed to respect or implement judicial accountability consistently (BATCH-0011-E008; BATCH-0011-E010; BATCH-0011-E014). Presidential appointments, removals, retirements, and reassignments of judges are documented, but the supplied evidence does not itself prove that they weakened independence (BATCH-0015-E006; BATCH-0019-E006). In the Goma case, forensic investigation, victim identification, witness access, appeals, and reparations were incomplete or disputed; the Kisangani compensation protest further shows unresolved victim remedy (BATCH-0011-E020; BATCH-0011-E021; BATCH-0022-E009). Thus, formal oversight and selected accountability existed, but credible independent investigation and delivered remedy were not established.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0029-E001","BATCH-0009-E004","BATCH-0011-E014","BATCH-0009-E005","BATCH-0019-E001","BATCH-0011-E021","BATCH-0022-E009"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0011-E008","BATCH-0011-E010","BATCH-0011-E020","BATCH-0015-E006","BATCH-0019-E006","BATCH-0011-E003"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Nationwide independence and effectiveness of courts, complaints bodies, and civilian oversight are not established.","The reparation fund’s 2023 staffing, disbursement, and geographic reach are unknown.","Many measures are attributed to government institutions or international partners rather than Tshisekedi personally.","Goma casualty and judicial findings remained disputed or incomplete.","The evidence does not prove that presidential judicial personnel decisions caused interference in specific cases."]},{"question_id":"3B.5","answer":"Exceptional powers were used broadly and only partly reviewed or narrowed. The state of siege, extended more than 50 times, transferred civilian administration to military and police authorities, subjected civilians to military courts, and was criticized for lacking meaningful public debate and required international derogation notification (BATCH-0012-R03-E001; BATCH-0012-R03-E003; BATCH-0012-R03-E007). Amnesty linked the regime to harassment and imprisonment of journalists, mass pretrial detention, restrictions on dissent, serious security-force abuses, and worsening attacks and displacement, although much of the outcome data spans 2021 onward and does not establish personal ordering of every abuse (BATCH-0009-E002; BATCH-0012-R03-E004). January 2023 police tear-gas dispersal and detention of protesters and journalists illustrate direct application of coercive powers in the target year (BATCH-0008-E008). Tshisekedi did convene an August roundtable to consider maintaining, requalifying, or lifting the regime and announced gradual easing in October, including ending a curfew and permitting peaceful demonstrations; the evidence does not show that the regime was repealed or that easing was fully implemented by year-end (BATCH-0007-E002; BATCH-0021-E012; BATCH-0008-E007). The revised press law retained possible imprisonment for press offenses, and Bujakera was detained under false-information, forgery, press, and penal provisions, without proof that Tshisekedi ordered the case (BATCH-0025-E007; BATCH-0025-E012). The record therefore supports expansive, rights-restrictive emergency administration with partial review and an unverified late corrective shift.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0012-R03-E001","BATCH-0012-R03-E003","BATCH-0012-R03-E007","BATCH-0009-E002","BATCH-0008-E008","BATCH-0025-E007","BATCH-0025-E012"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0007-E002","BATCH-0021-E012","BATCH-0008-E007","BATCH-0012-R03-E004"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The complete legal text, safeguards, legislative review, and geographic scope of extensions are not supplied.","The precise presidential role in each detention or military-court case is not established.","The roundtable’s recommendations and the implementation of announced easing are unknown.","The security counterfactual for the state of siege cannot be measured confidently.","The supplied evidence does not establish that surveillance or anti-terror powers were the legal basis for every cited prosecution."]},{"question_id":"3B.6","answer":"The evidence does not establish a lawful, proportionate reduction in exposure-adjusted violence. UNJHRO recorded 5,273 violations in 2023, a 12% decline from 2022, with conflict-province violations falling from 5,091 to 4,473; however, these are documented incidents, not total or exposure-adjusted violence, and reporting access may affect the trend (BATCH-0025-E009). Severe violence persisted: ADF attacks caused more than 1,000 reported fatalities, at least 1,211 civilians were killed in Ituri between January and October, and UNJHRO recorded at least 1,480 civilian victims of summary or extrajudicial killings in the first half, with armed groups responsible for most but state forces also contributing (BATCH-0027-E007; BATCH-0010-E015; BATCH-0011-E009). Sexual violence increased in eastern DRC, with displaced women and girls facing heightened rape and assault risks and limited access to support (BATCH-0008-E003; BATCH-0022-E012). Government cooperation with MONUSCO, Uganda, regional forces, IDP patrols, prosecutions, and ceasefire diplomacy were potentially protective, and an April ceasefire temporarily reduced hostilities, but the ceasefire later broke down, M23 expanded, and government support for aligned armed groups risked empowering adversaries (BATCH-0011-E010; BATCH-0016-E005; BATCH-0027-E006; BATCH-0028-E016). Amnesty assessed that the state of siege failed to meet its civilian-protection goals, but this is an attributed institutional assessment rather than an uncontested causal finding (BATCH-0012-R03-E004). The Goma operation added severe state-force violence against protesters, with disputed death figures and limited accountability (BATCH-0011-E018). Overall, the period shows widespread non-state and state-linked violence, with some protective activity but no demonstrated lawful safety improvement.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0025-E009","BATCH-0027-E007","BATCH-0010-E015","BATCH-0011-E009","BATCH-0008-E003","BATCH-0011-E010","BATCH-0016-E005"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0027-E006","BATCH-0028-E016","BATCH-0012-R03-E004","BATCH-0011-E018","BATCH-0011-E010"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The decline in documented violations is reporting-sensitive and not exposure-adjusted.","Conflict fatalities, displacement, sexual violence, and political violence are distinct outcomes and cannot be aggregated without a common denominator.","External armed groups, neighboring states, regional forces, and conflict geography constrain presidential causation.","The evidence does not provide a national ordinary-crime or fear-climate counterfactual.","The Goma operation supports state-force abuse but not necessarily direct presidential ordering."]},{"question_id":"3B.7","answer":"Protection of vulnerable groups was enacted and partly organized, but effective and equitable protection was not established. The government promulgated Indigenous-peoples and conflict-related sexual-violence protections, created victim services and reparations mechanisms, and reported GBV centers, mobile clinics, legal services, safe spaces, police patrols near IDP camps, and assistance to 9,500 women; these measures are formal, reported, or partner-supported and do not prove nationwide enforcement (BATCH-0001-E010; BATCH-0029-E002; BATCH-0011-E003; BATCH-0011-E006). UNFPA reported 2023 programme spending but government implementation shares of only 4% for GBV, 3% for gender and social norms, 3% for quality of care, and 14% for maternal-death reduction, limiting direct presidential attribution (BATCH-0029-E006). Humanitarian partners delivered substantial services, including more than 31,000 safe deliveries and mobile clinics, but these were UNFPA-supported outputs rather than demonstrated Tshisekedi-directed results (BATCH-0025-E003). Exposure remained severe: about 220,000 women were pregnant in eastern DRC amid fragile health infrastructure, sexual violence increased, displaced women and girls faced limited medical, psychosocial, legal, and economic support, and displacement reached roughly 6.9 million nationally (BATCH-0008-E002; BATCH-0008-E003; BATCH-0013-E014). Children and vulnerable populations also faced school closures, displacement, recruitment, discrimination, and limited services (BATCH-0022-E010; BATCH-0002-E022; BATCH-0010-E015). Forced evictions involving companies, police, military, and government authorities lacked effective grievance remedy, though personal presidential direction was not established (BATCH-0010-E018). The record therefore shows partial policy and service activity alongside widespread exposure, uneven access, and weakly verified enforcement.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0001-E010","BATCH-0029-E002","BATCH-0011-E003","BATCH-0011-E006","BATCH-0029-E006","BATCH-0008-E002","BATCH-0008-E003","BATCH-0022-E010"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0025-E003","BATCH-0013-E014","BATCH-0002-E022","BATCH-0010-E015","BATCH-0010-E018"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Government and partner funding, implementation, and outcomes cannot consistently be separated.","Several favorable measures are self-reported or formal and lack independent coverage and equity data.","Conflict and humanitarian evidence is regional and often does not establish personal presidential responsibility.","Implementation of the Indigenous-peoples law and reparations framework during 2023 is not demonstrated.","The record lacks a complete national measure for women, children, minorities, migrants, and persons with disabilities."]},{"question_id":"3B.8","answer":"Formal rights and some peaceful handling coexisted with recurring and severe restrictions. The legal framework recognized assembly and association, and Tshisekedi instructed authorities to protect electoral materials and punish violence and discrimination, but that directive did not itself establish protection for protest or dissent (BATCH-0011-E011; BATCH-0009-E001). Police blocked opposition gatherings, used tear gas and beatings, detained demonstrators and journalists, and restricted campaign movement; the May 20 march caused serious injuries, including to a child, while three officers were arrested without a reported final outcome (BATCH-0002-E011; BATCH-0002-E012; BATCH-0003-E003; BATCH-0003-E004). In January, police dispersed an unauthorized Goma protest and detained some protesters and journalists; in December, authorities banned an opposition march and deployed police and armored vehicles (BATCH-0008-E008; BATCH-0021-E009). The August 30 Goma operation was much more severe: authorities banned the demonstration, security forces killed dozens, injured many, and arrested more than 150; officers were convicted, but civilian prosecutions, forensic work, and remedies were criticized as incomplete (BATCH-0011-E018; BATCH-0011-E020; BATCH-0011-E021). Journalists and critics were also arrested or prosecuted, including Stanis Bujakera, and campaign-period security forces reportedly restricted opposition coverage (BATCH-0025-E012; BATCH-0002-E015). Qualifying evidence includes police escorting an October peaceful march and government assistance to an attacked journalist, but accountability for political-party attacks remained unresolved (BATCH-0022-E014; BATCH-0027-E002). Tshisekedi’s direct attribution is strongest for national security policy and his public praise of the police chief after the May operation; local and provincial responsibility is not automatically presidential.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0002-E011","BATCH-0003-E003","BATCH-0003-E004","BATCH-0008-E008","BATCH-0021-E009","BATCH-0011-E018","BATCH-0025-E012"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0011-E011","BATCH-0022-E014","BATCH-0027-E002","BATCH-0002-E012","BATCH-0009-E001"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The evidence does not show how consistently protests outside reported incidents were protected.","Goma casualty totals are disputed and the final accountability record is incomplete.","The direct presidential order for local restrictions or Goma killings is not established.","The legality of particular bans and the merits of individual charges remain partly unresolved.","Campaign-period journalist and opposition restrictions have incomplete chain-of-command evidence."]},{"question_id":"3B.9","answer":"Crisis response was mixed, with protective planning but serious failures, delayed assistance, and militarized enforcement. Tshisekedi chaired planning with MONUSCO and regional forces for ceasefire, disarmament, and civilian protection, ordered mixed army-police patrols for the Francophonie Games, convened a state-of-siege review, and supported reported GBV inquiries, camp patrols, and victim-protection measures (BATCH-0021-E001; BATCH-0018-E001; BATCH-0021-E012; BATCH-0011-E003). These are presidential directives, plans, or government reports; implementation, resource sufficiency, and protective outcomes are not consistently verified. Kwamouth violence killed at least 300 people and displaced more than 50,000; government reinforcement was delayed and assistance was inadequate, although personal presidential ordering is not shown (BATCH-0011-E001). Eastern conflict produced approximately 6.8–6.9 million internally displaced people, severe humanitarian access constraints, more than 25 million people in crisis or emergency food insecurity, and a $629.6 million WFP funding shortfall; these outcomes reflect conflict, donor constraints, and government capacity together (BATCH-0010-E003; BATCH-0013-E014; BATCH-0022-E013). In Goma, security forces used advance operational orders to suppress a banned protest, killed dozens, arrested civilians, and conducted incomplete investigations; some officers were convicted, but civilian prosecutions and remedies remained contested (BATCH-0011-E018; BATCH-0011-E019; BATCH-0011-E020; BATCH-0023-E014). Tshisekedi’s continued military rhetoric and recruitment appeals occurred amid stalled peace efforts and renewed fighting, but direct causal effects on domestic harm are unproven (BATCH-0007-E013; BATCH-0027-E006). The evidence supports materially adverse crisis management with partial corrective action, while distinguishing national strategy from provincial and unit-level attribution.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0021-E001","BATCH-0018-E001","BATCH-0021-E012","BATCH-0011-E001","BATCH-0013-E014","BATCH-0022-E013","BATCH-0011-E018","BATCH-0011-E019"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0011-E003","BATCH-0023-E014","BATCH-0007-E013","BATCH-0027-E006","BATCH-0010-E003"],"limitations_and_gaps":["National crisis-resource allocation and execution by exposure are not fully documented.","Several favorable measures are announced or self-reported rather than independently verified.","The president’s notice, approval, or corrective action concerning Kwamouth and Goma operations is incomplete.","Food insecurity and funding gaps have multiple causes and are not solely presidential outcomes.","The evidence does not establish nationwide systematic terror or a direct causal effect of rhetoric on violence."]},{"question_id":"3B.10","answer":"The evidence does not establish that people were durably safer from state and non-state violence by the end of 2023. UNJHRO recorded a 12% decline in documented violations, and ceasefire arrangements temporarily reduced M23 hostilities, but these signals are reporting-sensitive or temporary and do not demonstrate exposure-adjusted improvement (BATCH-0025-E009; BATCH-0027-E006). By late 2023, eastern conflict had produced roughly 6.8–6.9 million internally displaced people, M23 had expanded or retained territory, ADF attacks caused more than 1,000 reported fatalities, and renewed fighting increased political violence (BATCH-0010-E003; BATCH-0013-E014; BATCH-0027-E007; BATCH-0027-E006). Sexual violence and humanitarian access failures further demonstrate continued civilian exposure, especially for displaced women and girls (BATCH-0008-E003; BATCH-0022-E012; BATCH-0001-E020). Amnesty assessed that the state of siege failed its civilian-protection aims, while state forces themselves committed serious abuses; this is an attributed institutional assessment, not proof that every conflict outcome was personally caused by Tshisekedi (BATCH-0012-R03-E004; BATCH-0011-E009). The Goma killings, recurring detention and protest abuses, journalist repression, and reported government support for aligned armed groups show that state policy sometimes added risk rather than merely failing to prevent non-state violence (BATCH-0028-E015; BATCH-0028-E016; BATCH-0011-E018). Countervailing evidence includes joint operations, regional diplomacy, prosecutions, justice-capacity expansion, ICC cooperation, and the 2023 decline in documented violations, but these produced no verified durable national safety improvement or complete remedy (BATCH-0011-E010; BATCH-0009-E004; BATCH-0019-E001). The inherited baseline was already severe, with long-running eastern conflict and armed-group violence; therefore the end-state is best described as widespread recurring insecurity with significant state-attributed abuses and limited, uncertain improvement.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0025-E009","BATCH-0010-E003","BATCH-0013-E014","BATCH-0027-E007","BATCH-0008-E003","BATCH-0012-R03-E004","BATCH-0028-E016"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0027-E006","BATCH-0011-E010","BATCH-0009-E004","BATCH-0019-E001","BATCH-0011-E018","BATCH-0028-E015"],"limitations_and_gaps":["No complete exposure-adjusted inherited-to-2023 baseline or counterfactual is supplied.","Documented violations may be affected by reporting access, censorship, conflict geography, and humanitarian capacity.","Conflict fatalities, displacement, sexual violence, political violence, and state abuse are distinct measures and should not be treated as one outcome.","Presidential authority over armed groups, foreign forces, and decentralized provincial commands is incomplete.","The evidence shows limited accountability activity but not durable nationwide remedy or safety."]}],"cross_lens_observations":[]}
